import subprocess
import threading


def worker():
    subprocess.run(command)


command = ["pacman", "-Q", "r22-tglate-early"]
t = threading.Thread(target=worker)
command = ["pacman", "-S", "r22-tglate-late"]
t.start()
rationale: Python 3.14 semantics: worker contains no binding operation for command (no parameter, no assignment, no global/nonlocal declaration), so command is a free variable resolved in the module's global namespace, and name resolution of free variables occurs at runtime when worker executes, not when worker or the Thread object is defined (executionmodel.rst: free variable defined at lines 92-93; top-level names resolve by searching the global namespace at 138-143; 'Name resolution of free variables occurs at runtime, not at compile time' at 322). Thread.__init__ only stores self._target = worker (threading.py:925); Thread.start() 'arranges for the object's run() method to be invoked in a separate thread of control' (978-979), and run() invokes self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs) (1023-1024). Therefore worker() can only execute at or after the t.start() statement, which in program order is after the rebinding command = ['pacman','-S','r22-tglate-late']; the module namespace then holds exactly that binding and no later statement rebinds command. The single statically determined spawn is subprocess.run(['pacman','-S','r22-tglate-late']) -> host_mutation 'pacman -S r22-tglate-late' (shlex.join), observed, because the worker is unconditionally scheduled by start() and its argv is a fully literal module global at invocation time. Determining argv from a construction-time namespace snapshot ('pacman -Q r22-tglate-early') would misread late-bound globals; that early binding is passed to no call and is forbidden as an observed row.
